title: The Gate Evaluation Committee
subtitle: Who decides what happens at the Gates
summary: The independent body, founded by the University of Verna and now seated by all six powers, that classifies every Gate, clears every expedition and wrote the doctrine every Expeditioner learns at their first briefing.
content:
> *"The Committee never says yes. It says 'not yet', and then, eventually, 'cleared, subject to the above'."*
> — said among Expeditioners

The **Gate Evaluation Committee** decides what happens at the Gates. It evaluates and classifies every new Gate, keeps the records, clears expeditions, restricts dangerous Gates and orders quarantines. If an Expeditioner has stood in a queue, signed a manifest or been told *"did you touch the Core?"*, the Committee was somewhere behind it.

It was founded by the [[university-of-verna|University of Verna]], and for a time it was effectively a University committee. It is now a **separate body with members from all the factions**, and it, not the University, has the last word on the Gates. How that division of authority works in practice, and why the settlement itself answers to nobody, is told in [[who-runs-endros|Who Runs Endros?]]. The lessons its rules grew out of are in [[the-first-four-gates|Four Gates, Four Lessons]].

## From a University Committee to Everyone's Committee

When the first Gates began to form among the Valeoran Ruins, the University was already responsible for the Ruins, and the obvious thing was for it to evaluate the Gates as well. Its committee did the early surveys, wrote the early reports and, after the collapse of Gate One, issued the instruction that is still the oldest rule in Gate work: no Core is moved without explicit authorization.

The arrangement did not last. As the powers of the world arrived in Endros, a single university deciding who could enter a Gate, and what could be brought back, became impossible to defend. The committee was made independent, and each power was given a seat. The Archive's public sources do not record the exact terms, the date, or how hard the University argued; Vernans who were there tend to describe it as *the obvious next step*, in the tone people use for things that were not obvious at the time.

The University and the Committee are still rarely far apart. Many evaluators trained at the University, and much of the Committee's analysis happens in the [University of Verna Laboratories](outpost.html#university-of-verna-laboratories). But the decisions are made at the Committee's table.

## How the Committee Works

**The members.** The Committee seats one member for each of the six powers: Vardic, Aurelian, Vesperian, Kharadi, Tianzhao and Vernan. How each power chooses its member is its own business and differs from one to the next. The chair rotates among the seats, so no power presides for long.

**The evaluators.** The members decide; the **evaluators** do the work. They read the survey reports, examine returned Specimens, draft classifications, write the clearance conditions and give the briefings. They come from every faction, and many began as University researchers or as Expeditioners. An evaluator holds no seat and has no vote, which, the evaluators will tell you, is exactly what lets them say unwelcome things.

**The sub-committees.** Detailed questions go to smaller groups, of which the best known is the **classification sub-committee**, which reviews whether each Gate's classification is still accurate.

**What it decides.** Every Gate carries a classification, the status the Archive shows on each Gate record: *emerging*, *active*, *restricted*, *quarantined*, *dormant*, *collapsed*, *sealed* or *lost*. The Committee sets it, and it sets the terms of entry that follow from it: who may cross, with what equipment, under what reporting conditions, and what may be brought back.

> **Notice of Gate classification (standard form)**
>
> *Designation: ________ Classification: Restricted.*
>
> *Basis: findings on file. Entry requires expedition clearance. Returned material is to be treated as Specimens.*
>
> *Review: by the classification sub-committee, at intervals it determines.*
>
> *Note: a classification describes what is known at the date of issue. It is not a statement of safety.*

The last line is printed on every notice, whatever the classification. Expeditioners read it as a joke the first time and as advice afterwards.

How many members must agree for a decision to pass is not set out in the Committee's public papers. In practice it prefers not to decide until no member objects strongly, which is slow, and is also the point: a decision that has survived the whole table is one no single power can easily call illegitimate. A sense of what that table sounds like is preserved in the minutes quoted in [[who-runs-endros|Who Runs Endros?]].

## The Doctrine and Its Author

The Committee's best-known document is the **Gate Evaluation Doctrine**, the ten working assumptions under which it approaches every new Gate. They are listed in full in [[the-first-four-gates|Four Gates, Four Lessons]].

The Doctrine was drafted by [Anselm Hartree](characters.html#anselm-hartree), the Committee's **Senior Evaluator**. Hartree is Vernan, trained at the University, and one of the committee's first evaluators; when it became independent he stayed with it rather than return to the University. After the quarantine of Gate Four he set out what the first four Gates had taught, one assumption at a time, each traceable to a finding on file. The full Committee adopted the draft with fewer changes than anyone expected, which some Expeditioners take as proof that it was right, and others as proof that nobody had read it closely.

Hartree has never held the Vernan seat and, by his own account, does not want it. He still gives the first briefing to new Expeditioners whenever he can.

> **The first briefing, as new Expeditioners usually hear it**
>
> "Good morning. I am going to tell you ten things the Committee believes about the Gates. Please notice the word *believes*.
>
> "Number one: a Gate may remain stable indefinitely if its Core remains beyond the threshold. We believe this because the Green Vault has stayed open for as long as its Core has stayed inside it. That is evidence, not proof.
>
> "Number two: no Core is to be moved without explicit authorization. That one is not a belief. That one is a rule. Gate One is the reason, and Gate One no longer exists.
>
> "Questions? Good. Hold them until number seven, when you will have more."

*Evidence, not proof* is the phrase most associated with him. It appears in the Committee's documents often enough that Expeditioners say it back to him, and he has been heard to reply that he is glad someone was listening.

## The Committee and the Expeditioners

For Expeditioners, the Committee is the reason for most of the paperwork. Crews file manifests and equipment lists before they cross, hear the Doctrine before their first expedition, report what they found when they return, and hand everything they carried back to the intake counter as a Specimen. The [Expeditions](game.html#post-expeditions) rule covers what that means at the table.

The company that brings most of them to Endros, Nowhere Expeditions, wants the expeditions to keep running; the Committee wants each one to be justified. Neither says so in public, and both say so constantly in private.

> **Outside the Committee's offices, after an application was deferred**
>
> "We were ready to go this morning," said the Vardic crew leader.
>
> "I know," said the evaluator. "Your equipment list was excellent."
>
> "Then what's the problem?"
>
> "The Gate's classification is under review. If we clear you today and the review says *quarantined* tomorrow, we will have to decide whether you are allowed back."
>
> The crew leader considered this. "So when can we go?"
>
> "When we know what the door costs on the way out."

Most crews come to a working peace with it. The ones who have been inside a restricted Gate tend to defend it.

## What the Archive Does Not Know

The Committee's internal papers are not public. The Archive does not hold the terms under which it became independent, how each power selects its member, how votes are counted, or how a dispute between the Committee and a power's own government would be settled, since none has been publicly tested.
